A useful proof pattern is exchange: take an optimal solution and show how to replace one of its choices with the greedy choice without making the objective worse or destroying feasibility. Then solve the smaller remaining problem using the same argument. For maximum-cardinality interval scheduling, choosing the compatible interval that finishes first leaves at least as much future time as any other first interval. Replace the first interval in an optimal schedule with that earliest-finishing one. Every later interval that followed the old first interval can still follow the replacement, so cardinality does not decrease. At a graduate level, the answer is never just that the code ran. slides.narration: In Book III, Chapter 18, treat 18.2.2 Applying Greedy Graph Algorithms as an algorithmic claim. Kruskal’s minimum-spanning-tree algorithm sorts undirected edges by weight and accepts an edge only when its endpoints belong to different current components. A disjoint-set structure answers that connectivity question. Path compression shortens future searches, while union by rank prevents needlessly tall representative trees. The maintained forest has no cycles: accepting an edge between different components joins two trees. For correctness, consider the cut separating one current component from the others. A lightest eligible crossing edge can be exchanged into an appropriate minimum spanning tree without increasing total weight; removing an edge from the resulting cycle preserves a spanning tree. This safe-edge principle supports the greedy construction. At a graduate level, the answer is never just that the code ran. slides.narration: In Book III, Chapter 18, treat Failure clinic — Solving the wrong optimization problem as an algorithmic claim. An engineer replaces earliest finish with shortest duration because short jobs “use fewer resources.” The sample still returns the expected count, so the change is accepted. A later input contains one short interval in the middle that overlaps two mutually compatible longer intervals, and the revised rule loses a job. The mistake is not in sorting syntax; it is in replacing a proved choice rule with an intuition. A similar mismatch occurs when a minimum spanning tree is used to answer shortest-route queries. Connecting all sites cheaply may force a particular pair to travel along a long detour. The spanning-tree objective is global construction cost. A route query has a source, destination, and path-cost objective. The same graph can support both problems without making their outputs interchangeable. At a graduate level, the answer is never just that the code ran.
